title: Jeff Erickson, extra lecture notes for Algorithms (2013-2018)

locator_scheme: jeffe-notes:<file stem>.<section>, where <section> is the printed section number with the lecture prefix removed (01-random '1.4.1' -> 01-random.4.1; A-fft 'A.5' -> A-fft.5; 08-mincut prints its sections as 13.x -> 08-mincut.x; 98-induction and 99-recurrences use their bare section numbers).

concepts.name: Discrete probability spaces and events
concepts.statement: A discrete probability space is a countable sample space with a mass function Pr >= 0 summing to 1; events are subsets, combined by union, intersection, complement and conditioning, with independence defined by Pr[A and B] = Pr[A]Pr[B].
concepts.notes: 1.1.3 lists identities and inequalities incl. the union bound.

concepts.name: Random variables and linearity of expectation
concepts.statement: For any random variables X_i and constants a_i, E[sum a_i X_i] = sum a_i E[X_i], with no independence required; indicator variables turn counting questions into sums of probabilities.
concepts.notes: Section 1.2.1 is titled 'It is a fungus.'

concepts.name: Common distributions: uniform, Bernoulli, binomial, geometric
concepts.statement: The notes define the uniform, Bernoulli, binomial and geometric distributions with their expectations, e.g. a geometric variable with success probability p has expectation 1/p.

concepts.name: Removing bias from coin flips
concepts.statement: Flip a biased coin twice: output heads on HT, tails on TH, and retry on HH or TT; this yields a fair bit in 1/(p(1-p)) expected pairs (von Neumann), and a fair coin can simulate any known bias.

concepts.name: Coupon collecting (Pokemon collecting)
concepts.statement: Collecting all n equally likely types takes n*H_n = Theta(n log n) expected trials; after n trials the expected number of distinct types seen is about (1-1/e)n.

concepts.name: Generating random permutations (shuffling)
concepts.statement: Swapping each A[i] with a uniformly random element of A[1..i] (Fisher-Yates) produces every permutation with probability 1/n!, in O(n) time; plausible-looking variants are biased.
concepts.notes: 1.7 (properties of random permutations) is an unfinished outline.

concepts.name: The nuts and bolts problem
concepts.statement: Given n nuts and n bolts that can only be compared to each other, pick a random bolt, partition the nuts with it and the bolts with its matching nut, and recurse: expected O(n log n) comparisons, mirroring randomized quicksort.

concepts.name: Deterministic vs. randomized algorithms; expected running time
concepts.statement: A randomized algorithm's running time is a random variable; we bound its expectation for the worst-case input, separating Las Vegas algorithms (always correct) from Monte Carlo ones (probably correct).

concepts.name: Reductions to and from sorting
concepts.statement: Nuts and bolts and sorting reduce to each other, so randomized nuts-and-bolts matching needs Omega(n log n) comparisons and any deterministic O(n log n) solution would be hard to find.

concepts.name: Expected comparisons of randomized quicksort
concepts.statement: The i-th and j-th smallest elements are compared iff one of them is the first pivot chosen among ranks i..j, with probability 2/(j-i+1); summing gives at most 2n H_n = O(n log n) expected comparisons.
concepts.notes: 2.6 gives a recursive analysis, 2.7 the iterative (indicator) analysis, 2.8 an exact 'masochistic' solution.

concepts.name: Treaps
concepts.statement: A treap stores keys with priorities so that it is a binary search tree by key and a heap by priority; for distinct keys and priorities the treap is unique.

concepts.name: Treap insertion and deletion by rotations
concepts.statement: Insert as a leaf then rotate it up while its priority beats its parent's; delete by rotating the node down toward its higher-priority child until it is a leaf.

concepts.name: Random priorities give expected logarithmic depth
concepts.statement: With independent uniformly random priorities, node k is an ancestor of node i with probability 1/(|k-i|+1), so every node has expected depth at most 2 ln n + O(1).
concepts.notes: 3.1.4 notes the equivalence with randomized quicksort.

concepts.name: Skip lists
concepts.statement: Promote each element of a sorted linked list to the next level with probability 1/2; the expected number of levels is O(log n) and a search takes O(log n) expected time.

concepts.name: Markov's inequality
concepts.statement: For a non-negative random variable X and z > 0, Pr[X >= z] <= E[X]/z.

concepts.name: Chebyshev's inequality
concepts.statement: Pr[|X - E[X]| >= z] <= Var[X]/z^2; for sums of pairwise independent indicators the variance is at most the mean.
concepts.notes: 4.2 defines pairwise and k-wise independence; 4.4 higher moments.

concepts.name: Chernoff bounds
concepts.statement: For a sum X of independent indicator variables with mean mu, Pr[X >= (1+d)mu] <= (e^d/(1+d)^(1+d))^mu, and similar lower-tail bounds; deviations shrink exponentially in mu.

concepts.name: Treap depth with high probability
concepts.statement: Chernoff bounds show every node of a treap with random priorities has depth O(log n) with high probability, not just in expectation.

concepts.name: Hash tables: the dictionary problem
concepts.statement: A hash table stores n items from a large universe U in an array of m slots using a hash function h: U -> {0..m-1}; the load factor is n/m, and collisions must be resolved.

concepts.name: Universal hash families
concepts.statement: Any fixed hash function has bad inputs, so h is chosen at random from a family; the family is universal if Pr[h(x)=h(y)] <= 1/m for all x != y.
concepts.notes: 5.2 'The Importance of Being Random', 5.3 '...But Not Too Random'.

concepts.name: Hashing with chaining
concepts.statement: With each slot holding a linked list and h drawn from a universal family, the expected length of the chain for any key is at most 1 + n/m, so operations take O(1 + n/m) expected time.

concepts.name: Multiplicative hashing
concepts.statement: h_a(x) = (a x mod p) mod m with random a, and the binary variant ((a x) mod 2^w) >> (w - l), give (nearly) universal families that are fast to evaluate.

concepts.name: Balls and bins: maximum chain length
concepts.statement: Throwing n balls into n bins uniformly, the fullest bin holds O(log n / log log n) balls with high probability.

concepts.name: Perfect hashing (two-level)
concepts.statement: For a static set, hash into n primary buckets and give each bucket of size n_i a collision-free secondary table of size n_i^2; expected total space is O(n) and lookups take O(1) worst-case time.

concepts.name: Open addressing and linear/binary probing
concepts.statement: Open addressing stores items in the table itself and probes a sequence of slots; linear probing scans consecutive slots, and binary probing (a variant analyzed in the notes) gives O(1) expected probes when the load factor is bounded below 1.

concepts.name: Cuckoo hashing
concepts.statement: Each key lives in one of two slots h1(x) or h2(x); insertion evicts occupants along a path and rebuilds on long cycles, giving worst-case O(1) lookups and expected O(1) insertions at load below 1/2.

concepts.name: Bloom filters
concepts.statement: Represent a set by an m-bit array and k hash functions, setting bits h_1(x)..h_k(x) on insertion; queries never give false negatives and the false-positive rate is about (1 - e^{-kn/m})^k, minimized near k = (m/n) ln 2.

concepts.name: The streaming model
concepts.statement: A streaming algorithm reads a long sequence once and must answer queries about it using space much smaller than the stream.

concepts.name: Count-min sketch
concepts.statement: Keep d rows of w counters with independent hash functions; estimating a frequency as the minimum of its d counters never underestimates and overestimates by more than eps*N with probability at most delta when w = e/eps and d = ln(1/delta).

concepts.name: Brute-force string matching
concepts.statement: Checking every shift of pattern P[1..m] against text T[1..n] takes O(mn) time in the worst case.

concepts.name: Karp-Rabin fingerprinting
concepts.statement: Treat strings as base-sigma numbers reduced mod a random prime q; rolling the fingerprint of each text window in O(1) time finds all matches in O(n + m) expected time with a small false-positive probability.

concepts.name: String matching with a finite-state machine
concepts.statement: Redundant comparisons can be avoided by a finite-state machine whose state is the length of the longest pattern prefix that is a suffix of the text read so far; with failure links this is the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, running in O(n) after preprocessing.

concepts.name: Computing the KMP failure function
concepts.statement: The failure function fail[j] (the longest proper prefix of P[1..j-1] that is also a suffix) can be computed in O(m) time by running the matcher on the pattern against itself; an optimized version skips states that would compare the same character.

concepts.name: Global minimum cut and edge contraction
concepts.statement: A minimum cut of a connected multigraph is a smallest set of edges whose removal disconnects it; contracting an edge merges its endpoints, keeps parallel edges and never decreases the minimum cut.

concepts.name: Karger's contraction algorithm
concepts.statement: Contracting uniformly random edges until two vertices remain returns a particular minimum cut with probability at least 2/(n(n-1)); repeating O(n^2 log n) times finds a minimum cut with high probability.

concepts.name: Karger-Stein recursive contraction
concepts.statement: Contract to about n/sqrt(2) vertices twice independently and recurse on each; success probability is Omega(1/log n) and the running time is O(n^2 log n), so O(n^2 log^3 n) gives high probability.

concepts.name: Amortized analysis: the binary counter
concepts.statement: Amortized cost bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations rather than each one; incrementing a binary counter costs O(log n) in the worst case but n increments flip only O(n) bits in total.

concepts.name: Summation, taxation and charging methods
concepts.statement: Bound total cost by summing over operations, by charging each operation a fixed 'tax' that prepays future work, or by charging each unit of work to an earlier event that pays for it.

concepts.name: The potential method
concepts.statement: Define a non-negative potential Phi on data-structure states with Phi(initial)=0; the amortized cost of an operation is its actual cost plus the change in Phi, and total amortized cost bounds total actual cost.

concepts.name: Incrementing and decrementing counters
concepts.statement: Alternating between 2^k and 2^k - 1 makes a standard binary counter cost Theta(k) per operation; representing the value as P - N with bit strings P AND N = 0 gives O(1) amortized increments and decrements.

concepts.name: Gray codes
concepts.statement: A Gray code lists all 2^n bit strings so consecutive strings differ in one bit (binary reflected Gray code); it can be generated with O(1) bit flips per step.
concepts.notes: 9.5 discusses generalities and pitfalls of amortization.

concepts.name: Lazy deletion and global rebuilding
concepts.statement: Mark deleted nodes instead of removing them and rebuild the whole tree perfectly balanced once half the nodes are marked; rebuilding costs O(n) but is amortized O(1) per deletion.

concepts.name: Scapegoat trees
concepts.statement: Keep the tree alpha-weight-balanced lazily: after an insertion makes the tree too deep, rebuild the subtree of the highest unbalanced ancestor (the scapegoat); operations take O(log n) amortized time.

concepts.name: Rotations, double rotations and splaying
concepts.statement: Splaying moves a node to the root by zig, zig-zig and zig-zag (double) rotations, roughly halving the depth of every node on the access path.

concepts.name: Splay trees
concepts.statement: A splay tree splays every accessed node to the root; by the Access Lemma (potential = sum of log subtree sizes) every operation takes O(log n) amortized time.
concepts.notes: 10.7 (static optimality, working set) and 10.8 (dynamic optimality conjecture) follow.

concepts.name: Disjoint sets with reversed trees
concepts.statement: The union-find ADT supports MakeSet, Find (return the set's leader) and Union; storing each set as a reversed tree whose root is the leader, with union by rank (or depth), gives O(log n) worst-case Find.

concepts.name: Shallow threaded trees
concepts.statement: Giving every element a direct pointer to its leader makes Find O(1); merging the smaller set into the larger makes Union O(log n) amortized.

concepts.name: Path compression
concepts.statement: During Find, point every visited node directly at the root; combined with union by rank, any m operations on n elements take O(m log* n) time, and in fact O(m alpha(m,n)).
concepts.notes: 11.4 proves O(log* n); 11.5 'turning the crank' iterates the argument.

concepts.name: The Ackermann function and its inverse
concepts.statement: Iterating the log*-style argument shows union by rank with path compression runs in O(m alpha(n)) time, where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, at most 4 for any practical n.

concepts.name: Decision-tree lower bounds
concepts.statement: A comparison algorithm corresponds to a decision tree whose internal nodes are queries and leaves are outputs; its worst-case running time is at least the tree's depth.

concepts.name: Information-theoretic lower bound
concepts.statement: A decision tree with branching factor k that must distinguish N outcomes has depth at least log_k N; e.g. searching a sorted array needs Omega(log n) comparisons. Hashing escapes it by asking queries with more than O(1) outcomes.
concepts.notes: 12.4 'But wait a second...' explains the hashing loophole.

concepts.name: Comparison sorting needs Omega(n log n)
concepts.statement: Any comparison sort must distinguish n! permutations, so its decision tree has depth at least log_2 n! = Omega(n log n).

concepts.name: Finding the maximum needs n-1 comparisons
concepts.statement: Every element other than the maximum must lose at least one comparison, so any algorithm needs n-1 comparisons; an adversary argument makes this precise.

concepts.name: Adversary arguments
concepts.statement: To prove a lower bound, imagine an adversary that answers queries consistently but so as to keep the answer undetermined as long as possible (three-card and n-card monte).
concepts.notes: Sections 13.1 and 13.2; 13.3 finds the pattern 01 in bit strings.

concepts.name: Evasive graph properties
concepts.statement: A graph property is evasive if every algorithm must query all n(n-1)/2 edge slots in the worst case; connectedness is evasive by an adversary that answers 'no edge' unless that would disconnect the graph.

concepts.name: Finding the minimum and maximum: ceil(3n/2) - 2
concepts.statement: Pairing elements and comparing winners and losers finds both min and max in ceil(3n/2) - 2 comparisons, and an adversary argument shows this is optimal.
concepts.notes: 13.8 gives a lower bound for median finding.

concepts.name: Proof by smallest counterexample
concepts.statement: To prove P(n) for all n, suppose some n fails and take the smallest such n; deriving a smaller counterexample is a contradiction (shown by proving every integer > 1 has a prime divisor).

concepts.name: The axiom of induction and strong induction
concepts.statement: If P(0) holds and P(k) for all k < n implies P(n), then P(n) holds for all natural numbers; the inductive hypothesis may assume all smaller cases (strong induction).
concepts.notes: 3 'Stamps and Recursion' shows that induction proofs and recursive algorithms are the same thing.

concepts.name: Induction on numbers, summations and tilings
concepts.statement: Worked induction proofs: closed forms for summations, tiling a 2^n x 2^n board minus one square with L-triominoes, existence of binary representations, Fibonacci parity.

concepts.name: Induction on recursive functions and trees
concepts.statement: Properties of recursively defined functions and of trees are proved by induction following the recursive definition (e.g. on the subtrees of a full binary tree).

concepts.name: Solving recurrences by guess and confirm
concepts.statement: Guess a closed form (from small cases or a recursion tree) and prove it by induction, adjusting constants or lower-order terms when the induction fails; worked for Hanoi, Fibonacci and mergesort.

concepts.name: Divide-and-conquer recurrences by recursion trees
concepts.statement: For T(n) = rT(n/c) + f(n), the level sums form a series that is decreasing (root dominates), constant (Theta(f(n) log n)) or increasing (leaves dominate, Theta(n^{log_c r})).

concepts.name: The Akra-Bazzi method
concepts.statement: For T(n) = sum a_i T(n/b_i) + f(n), let rho satisfy sum a_i b_i^{-rho} = 1; then T(n) = Theta(n^rho (1 + integral_1^n f(u)/u^{rho+1} du)).

concepts.name: Linear recurrences by annihilators
concepts.statement: Write the recurrence with shift operators; the operator that annihilates the sequence factors as a product of (E - c) terms, and each factor (E - c)^k contributes a term polynomial(n) * c^n to the solution.
concepts.notes: Section 6 covers domain and range transformations.

concepts.name: Polynomial representations
concepts.statement: A degree-(n-1) polynomial can be stored by its n coefficients, by its values at n distinct points, or by its roots; each makes different operations (evaluate, add, multiply) cheap.

concepts.name: Converting by Vandermonde matrices
concepts.statement: Evaluating at n points is multiplication by the Vandermonde matrix and interpolation by its inverse; done naively these take O(n^2) time.

concepts.name: The fast Fourier transform
concepts.statement: Evaluating at the n-th roots of unity splits p(x) = p_even(x^2) + x p_odd(x^2) into two half-size problems at the (n/2)-th roots, giving the DFT in O(n log n) time.

concepts.name: Inverting the FFT
concepts.statement: The inverse DFT is the DFT with conjugate roots of unity divided by n, so interpolation from values at roots of unity also takes O(n log n).

concepts.name: Fast polynomial multiplication
concepts.statement: Multiply two polynomials by FFT to values, pointwise multiplication, and inverse FFT, in O(n log n) time.
concepts.notes: A.9 describes the iterative radix-2 butterfly network.

concepts.name: Faster exponential algorithms for 3SAT
concepts.statement: Branching on the literals of a short clause (with simplification) solves 3SAT in O(c^n poly(n)) time for c < 2, e.g. a recurrence like T(n) <= T(n-1)+T(n-2)+T(n-3) gives about 1.84^n.

concepts.name: Faster exponential algorithms for maximum independent set
concepts.statement: Branching on a vertex of high degree (exclude it, or include it and delete its neighbours), with simple rules for low-degree vertices, gives MIS in O(c^n) time for c well below 2.
concepts.notes: B.3 (dynamic programming, Held-Karp TSP) is a stub.

concepts.name: DFA minimization by dynamic programming
concepts.statement: Two DFA states are distinguishable iff some string leads one to accept and the other to reject; filling the distinguishability table by string length computes the minimal DFA in polynomial time.

concepts.name: NFA acceptance and regular-expression matching
concepts.statement: Whether an NFA (or a regular expression, via an equivalent NFA or a direct recurrence on subexpressions) accepts a string of length n is decided by DP over (position, state) in polynomial time.

concepts.name: Context-free parsing (CYK)
concepts.statement: For a grammar in Chomsky normal form, whether a nonterminal derives each substring is computed by DP over substring intervals in O(n^3) time.

concepts.name: Saving space by divide and conquer (Hirschberg)
concepts.statement: An optimal edit-distance alignment can be recovered in O(mn) time and O(m + n) space by finding where the optimal path crosses the middle row and recursing on both halves.

concepts.name: Saving time with sparseness
concepts.statement: When few table entries matter (e.g. few matching character pairs in LCS), the DP can be computed from those key entries only, in time near-linear in their number.

concepts.name: Monotone optimal roots (Knuth's speedup)
concepts.statement: For optimal binary search trees, OptRoot[i, j-1] <= OptRoot[i, j] <= OptRoot[i+1, j], which limits each minimization and reduces the time from O(n^3) to O(n^2).

concepts.name: Total monotonicity and the SMAWK algorithm
concepts.statement: In a totally monotone matrix the row minima can be found in O(m + n) time by SMAWK (reduce columns, recurse on even rows, interpolate odd rows), which speeds up many DPs.

concepts.name: The Four Russians speedup
concepts.statement: Precomputing all small t x t blocks of a DP table with tiny alphabets, for t = Theta(log n), cuts the work by a factor of about log^2 n (e.g. edit distance in O(n^2 / log n)).

concepts.name: Matroids and the greedy algorithm
concepts.statement: A matroid is a ground set with a non-empty family of independent sets closed under subsets and satisfying the exchange property; for every weight function the greedy algorithm finds a maximum-weight basis exactly when the structure is a matroid.

concepts.name: Scheduling unit jobs with deadlines
concepts.statement: Sets of unit-time jobs that can all meet their deadlines form a matroid, so greedily taking jobs in decreasing profit order while feasible maximizes total profit.

concepts.name: Unbalanced flows: supplies and demands
concepts.statement: Generalize flows by giving each vertex a balance (supply or demand) and edges lower and upper bounds; feasibility reduces to one maximum flow from a super-source to a super-sink.

concepts.name: Pseudoflows and augmenting between imbalances
concepts.statement: A pseudoflow respects capacities but not conservation; repeatedly pushing flow along residual paths from excess to deficit vertices yields a feasible flow if one exists.
concepts.notes: F.4: two-stage variations (feasible flow, then max flow in the residual graph).

concepts.name: Minimum-cost circulations and cycle canceling
concepts.statement: A circulation is minimum-cost iff its residual graph has no negative-cost cycle; repeatedly canceling negative cycles (found by Bellman-Ford) terminates with an optimal integral circulation.

concepts.name: Successive shortest paths
concepts.statement: Augmenting along cheapest residual paths from supply to demand vertices maintains a minimum-cost flow at every step.

concepts.name: Node potentials and reduced costs
concepts.statement: With potentials pi equal to shortest-path distances, the reduced costs c(u->v) + pi(u) - pi(v) are non-negative, so each successive-shortest-path step can use Dijkstra.
concepts.notes: G.4 covers transshipment and transportation problems.

concepts.name: Linear programming
concepts.statement: A linear program maximizes or minimizes a linear objective over the points satisfying a finite set of linear inequalities; in canonical form: maximize c.x subject to Ax <= b, x >= 0.

concepts.name: The geometry of linear programs
concepts.statement: The feasible region is a convex polyhedron; a bounded feasible LP attains its optimum at a vertex, and an LP may be infeasible or unbounded.

concepts.name: Formulating problems as linear programs
concepts.statement: Shortest paths, maximum flows and minimum cuts (and many other problems) can be written as linear programs.

concepts.name: Linear programming duality
concepts.statement: Every LP has a dual whose feasible solutions bound the primal (weak duality); if either has an optimum, both do and the optima are equal (strong duality), proved via the fundamental theorem / Farkas-type separation.

concepts.name: Complementary slackness
concepts.statement: Feasible primal x and dual y are both optimal iff every primal variable that is positive has a tight dual constraint and every dual variable that is positive has a tight primal constraint.

concepts.name: The simplex algorithm
concepts.statement: Starting from a feasible basis, the simplex algorithm repeatedly pivots to an adjacent basis that improves the objective until the current vertex is locally, hence globally, optimal.
concepts.notes: I.1 defines bases, feasibility and local optimality; I.3 finds an initial basis.

concepts.name: Network simplex
concepts.statement: For flow LPs, bases correspond to spanning trees and pivots to exchanging tree edges, giving a combinatorial version of simplex for minimum-cost flows.

concepts.name: Linear expected time in fixed dimension
concepts.statement: A randomized incremental algorithm (Seidel) solves an LP with n constraints in d variables in O(d! n) expected time.

concepts.name: Approximation algorithms and ratios
concepts.statement: An algorithm is an alpha-approximation if on every instance its output is within a factor alpha of the optimum (A(X) <= alpha OPT(X) for minimization); proofs compare against a lower bound on OPT.

concepts.name: Greedy load balancing
concepts.statement: Assigning each job to the currently least-loaded machine gives makespan at most 2 OPT; sorting jobs in decreasing order first improves this to 3/2 OPT (and in fact 4/3 - 1/(3m)).

concepts.name: Vertex cover approximation
concepts.statement: Greedily taking a vertex of maximum degree is an O(log n)-approximation; the 'obviously stupid' rule of taking both endpoints of any remaining edge is a 2-approximation, essentially the best known, and extends to hitting set.

concepts.name: Greedy set cover and hitting set
concepts.statement: Repeatedly choosing the set that covers the most uncovered elements is an H_n = O(log n) approximation for set cover (and for hitting set).

concepts.name: LP rounding for weighted vertex cover
concepts.statement: Solve the LP relaxation and take every vertex with x*(v) >= 1/2; the result is a vertex cover of weight at most 2 OPT. Randomized rounding (take v with probability x*(v), repeated) gives O(log n) for set cover.

concepts.name: Traveling salesman: hardness and metric approximation
concepts.statement: General TSP has no polynomial-time approximation within any factor unless P=NP, but for metric TSP doubling an MST and shortcutting gives a 2-approximation (Christofides improves to 3/2).

concepts.name: k-center clustering
concepts.statement: Gonzalez's algorithm picks each next center as the point farthest from the current centers, giving a 2-approximation; doing better than 2 is NP-hard.

concepts.name: An FPTAS for subset sum
concepts.statement: Trimming the list of reachable sums so that no two kept values are within a factor (1 + eps/2n) gives a (1 - eps)-approximation in time polynomial in n and 1/eps.
